text_blocks.snippet: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is characterized by a rapid decline in kidney function, leading to the inability to adequately filter waste products from the blood. The pathophysiology is complex and involves a combination of hemodynamic instability, inflammation, cellular damage, and altered renal blood flow. Understanding these processes is crucial for developing effective prevention and treatment strategies.
snippet_highlighted_words: a combination of hemodynamic instability, inflammation, cellular damage, and altered renal blood flow

list.title: Reduced Renal Blood Flow:
list.snippet: Ischemia (reduced blood flow) and hypoxia (low oxygen) are primary drivers of AKI. This can result from various factors like hypovolemia (low blood volume), sepsis, or renal artery stenosis. Reduced blood flow leads to impaired glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and cellular damage within the kidney.

list.title: Endothelial Dysfunction:
list.snippet: The endothelium, which lines blood vessels, plays a critical role in regulating blood flow and inflammation. AKI can cause endothelial dysfunction, leading to further disruptions in renal blood flow and promoting inflammation.

list.title: Inflammation:
list.snippet: Inflammatory responses are a significant component of AKI. The immune system is activated, leading to the release of inflammatory mediators (cytokines and chemokines) and the infiltration of immune cells into the kidney. This inflammation can exacerbate cellular damage and contribute to the progression of AKI.
